e.t: This Greek LXX noun refers to “words” or “records,” describing spoken statements or written accounts. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 4:22. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, the precise sense intended in that occurrence cannot be narrowed further. Its basic meaning remains a reference to words or records rather than an action, quality, or person.

This Greek LXX noun refers to glory or delight—something honored, treasured, or pleasing. Its central sense points to an object or reality that brings admiration or gladness. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, in two passages of Isaiah and once in 2 Maccabees. Since the available material does not include the surrounding verse text, the exact force of the word in each passage must be understood from its immediate context.

Adaia is a proper name, rendered “Adaia” and also associated with “Athea.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, appearing in genealogical and community records in Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. Since it is a personal name, its meaning in any particular passage depends mainly on which individual bears it there.

This word means “air,” the invisible atmosphere surrounding and supporting ordinary life. It is a noun describing the air itself, and it can also function descriptively in relation to something connected with air. Within the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 10 times, including passages from 2 Samuel, Psalms, Wisdom, and 2 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains physical and straightforward; the surrounding verse determines whether the air is being described as a place, medium, or condition.

This word means “rooster,” the male domestic fowl. It is a noun naming the bird itself, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 30:31. The word’s basic meaning is therefore clear and concrete: it identifies a rooster. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself refers simply to this kind of bird.

Amal is a proper name, rendered as “Amal.” It identifies a named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:35. The available information establishes the name and its location, but does not provide the surrounding verse text or additional details about the person. Thus, its ordinary lexical meaning is simply the personal name Amal.

This word refers to someone who is crippled—someone with a serious physical limitation. It can function as an adjective describing such a person or condition, and as a noun referring to the person themselves. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 8:24. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains a plain description of physical disability.

This adjective means “innumerable”: too many to be counted or numbered. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes something present in such great quantity that counting it is impossible or impractical. The word occurs 13 times in the LXX, including passages in 1 Kings, Job, Proverbs, Joel, and several deuterocanonical books. Its central idea remains consistent wherever it appears: an immense number or multitude beyond ordinary counting.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “draw out,” describing the act of bringing something out from a source. It is an action word rather than a name or description of a person. The word appears six times in the Greek Old Testament, from Genesis through Isaiah, showing a repeated use for an act of drawing out. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being drawn and the surrounding sentence. This LXX word should be understood as a Greek Old Testament entity, distinct from Greek New Testament vocabulary.

gl: restore order by clearing away; clear away
d: restore order by clearing away; clear away

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means to “restore order by clearing away” or to “clear away.” It describes removing what is out of place so that order is restored. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 4:38. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is the active removal of disorder or unwanted things.

Apollonios is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. It is rendered as “Apollōnios; Apollonios,” preserving the individual’s name. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the name occurs 19 times, from 1 Maccabees 3:10 through 4 Maccabees 4:13. The name appears across 1, 2, and 4 Maccabees, but its precise reference in any particular passage must be determined from that passage’s surrounding text.

This adjective means “inactive; fallow,” describing something that is not working, being used, or producing activity. It can refer to an unworked condition, such as land left uncultivated, or more generally to something idle rather than active. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times across 1 Kings, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “ploughshare,” the working part of a plough that cuts into and turns the soil. It is a noun naming an agricultural tool rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Judges 3:31, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The word refers specifically to a tool used in cultivating ground.

This adjective describes something that is not liable to decay or rot. It points to a quality of resistance to deterioration, especially when describing a material or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 16 times, all in 16 Old Testament verses, most often in Exodus, with additional occurrences in Deuteronomy and Isaiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the noun and surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains something that does not readily perish through decay.

This adjective means “ephemeral,” describing something that lasts only briefly or is short-lived. It points to temporary existence rather than something lasting or enduring. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 7:1, so its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic meaning remains clear: the word characterizes a person, condition, or period as limited in duration and soon passing away.

This noun means “blight,” a harmful condition that damages or ruins plants or crops. It names an affliction rather than an action, describing the destructive effect itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Haggai 2:17. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but the word’s central sense remains a damaging blight affecting what should grow and produce. This is a distinct Greek LXX word, preserved here in its Old Testament setting.

This Greek LXX word means “profane.” It describes a person or thing as profane and can also function as a noun for someone or something so described. In ordinary Bible language, it identifies what is regarded as profane rather than holy. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, with “profane” also appearing as its English rendering. Its precise force in any verse depends on that passage’s context.

Bēthdagōn, also rendered Viththagon, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament corpus. The name occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 10:83. Because no verse text or further contextual evidence is available here, its precise referent and significance cannot be explained beyond recognizing it as this proper name.

This Greek LXX verb means “referee,” describing the action of serving as a referee. It presents refereeing as an activity rather than naming the person who performs it. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom 10:12. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s precise role in that sentence must be understood from the passage itself. Its basic meaning remains the action of refereeing.

Gaddi; Gaththi is a proper name used for people in the Greek Old Testament and related biblical history. It identifies individuals rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. The name occurs twelve times in the Greek LXX corpus, beginning in Numbers and continuing through 1 Maccabees. Since it is a personal name, its meaning is chiefly its identifying function: it distinguishes a particular person in each passage. The precise person identified depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means “Gather” and functions as a proper name in the Greek LXX. It appears once in the LXX corpus, in Genesis 10:23. The available lexical meaning identifies the name’s basic sense, while the reference locates its single occurrence. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s particular role in that passage cannot be described further without adding details not provided by Scripture in this record.

Gothni is a proper name—the personal name of an individual mentioned in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or spiritual concept; it identifies a person. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at 1 Chronicles 26:7. Without the verse text and its surrounding passage, the person’s specific role or significance cannot be stated reliably from the name alone.

This verb means “lay waste a country.” It describes an action directed toward a country, rather than naming a person, place, or object. Its basic meaning concerns the act itself, not a separate title or description. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 2:14. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, since the verse text is not included here.

This verb means to declare property public and confiscate it. It describes an official action in which someone’s possessions are taken into public ownership or seized by authority. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 3:96, so its normal meaning is clear even though the wider context is not included here. The word focuses on the formal taking of property, not merely on borrowing, damaging, or privately stealing it.

This noun means “double” or “doubling”: it refers to something given, measured, or understood as twice as much as another amount. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in Job 42:10, so its exact force there must be understood from the surrounding verse rather than from the word alone. Its central idea is increase to twice the former measure, not merely a general increase.

This Greek LXX noun means “quoit,” a flat, ring-shaped object used in a throwing game. It names the object itself rather than an action or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 4:14. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its ordinary meaning is the physical game object called a quoit.

The word means “setting.” It is a noun used to name a setting rather than describe an action as a verb. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, it occurs 20 times across 18 verses. Its precise sense in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central lexical idea remains “setting.”

Ednas, also rendered Ethnas, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 2 Chronicles 17:14. Because it is a proper name, its meaning lies chiefly in identifying a particular person, not in conveying a broader idea that can be applied across many passages. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain that person’s specific role there.

This verb means “teach thoroughly”: it describes giving instruction in a complete or careful way rather than merely making a brief statement. As a verb, it expresses the action of instructing someone. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times, so its normal sense is focused and consistent rather than broad or frequent. The surrounding wording determines what is being taught and to whom, but the word itself emphasizes thorough instruction.

This noun means a “free-will offering”—a gift presented voluntarily rather than because someone is compelled to give it. It describes an offering whose defining feature is willing generosity. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Ezra 7:16. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning points to a freely chosen contribution offered to God or for sacred purposes.

This is a proper name, rendered “Elidae” and also given as “Elithae.” It identifies a named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 5:16. The available wording identifies the name but does not provide a further lexical sense, so its clearest function is to name someone in that passage.

This word means “my God,” expressing a personal address to God. It is a noun, used as a direct designation rather than as an action or description. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Samuel 1:11. Its possessive wording presents God as the one being personally called upon or acknowledged by the speaker. The precise force of the expression in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is clear: “my God.”

This Greek LXX verb means “initiate” or “begin.” It describes starting an action, undertaking, or period rather than continuing something already underway. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 11 times, including passages in Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees. Its ordinary sense is straightforward: to set something in motion or enter upon it. The exact force in a particular verse depends on what action or period the surrounding sentence identifies.

This noun means “shaking,” describing a physical movement or trembling. It names the act or condition of being shaken rather than a person, object, or command. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 22:13. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its context, but its central sense remains movement marked by shaking or trembling. It is a Greek LXX word and should be understood as distinct from Greek New Testament word entities.

This Greek LXX verb means “renew” or “restore”: to make something new again or bring it back to an earlier condition. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 10:44. The reference identifies its sole occurrence, but without the verse text the particular object being renewed or restored cannot be stated responsibly.

This Greek noun means “commission,” referring to an authorization or assignment given to someone. It names a charge entrusted to a person rather than an action they perform themselves. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 13:14. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the central idea remains an official commission or entrusted responsibility.

This Greek LXX noun means a “tool” or “instrument”—an object used for carrying out a task. It refers broadly to an implement rather than to a person, action, or quality. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, all in Exodus, where it is associated with the instruments used in the tabernacle’s service. Its exact reference in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains an implement or useful object.

This word means “kid,” referring to a young goat. It is a noun used for an actual animal in the Greek Old Testament translation, including goats selected for food, sacrifice, or other ordinary uses. The word occurs 24 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books represented in this corpus, with occurrences reaching from Genesis through Song of Songs. Its basic meaning remains the same wherever it appears; the surrounding passage determines the kid’s particular role in that verse.

This noun refers to a wish expressed before God or to a vow—a solemn promise made to him. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used especially for promises or commitments that a person makes and is expected to honor. It occurs 81 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, with frequent use in Numbers and other passages concerning vows. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Ēnia” or “Inia.” It identifies a named individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice: once in Nahum 2:4 and once in 1 Maccabees 6:28. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself gives the person’s identity but does not establish what that individual is doing or why the person matters in either passage.

This Greek LXX verb means to have courage—to be brave, confident, or encouraged rather than overcome by fear. It describes a call or condition of inner strength. The word appears three times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Daniel and 4 Maccabees, so its basic sense is consistent across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical settings. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding words and situation.

Thēzia, also rendered Thizia, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, in Nehemiah 11:5. Without the surrounding verse text, its personal significance and role in that passage cannot be explained further; the supported meaning is simply the individual’s name.

Iaziel, also written Iazil, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 24:23. Because it is a proper name and no verse text is supplied here, its significance is identifying the person who bears the name, while the surrounding passage provides the details about that person. The name’s ordinary meaning is therefore its use as a personal designation: Iaziel or Iazil.

Ἰεζραηλῖτις is a proper name or designation rendered “Iezraēlitis” or “Iezrelitis.” It identifies a person by this distinctive name or association, rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, appearing in passages connected with the families and household relationships of David. The exact person identified depends on the surrounding verse, but the word itself functions as a personal designation. It is distinctively preserved here as a Greek LXX term.

Jerusalem is the name of a city. In the Greek Old Testament, this word consistently identifies Jerusalem as a recognized place, rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs 727 times across the LXX corpus, including both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. The word appears throughout historical, prophetic, and poetic writings, showing its broad use as a place-name in biblical language. Its exact significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and context.

Ikam is a proper name, preserved as “Ikam.” It identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:22. Because the available wording gives only the name and no verse text or surrounding context, its specific identity cannot be described more narrowly from this lexical entry alone.

Ira is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 11:40, and is rendered “Ira.” Because the available passage information does not include the verse text or surrounding context, the name itself does not provide a broader meaning beyond identifying the person who bears it. Its precise role in that passage must be understood from the surrounding biblical context.

Kadēmōth, also rendered Kathimoth, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 6:64. The name itself does not provide enough information to identify whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity; that determination requires the surrounding verse and passage. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the name of a specific biblical referent.

This noun refers to the character and conduct of a person—the qualities shown in who someone is and how that person behaves. It brings inner character and outward conduct together as one subject. The word occurs five times in the Greek LXX corpus, all in 4 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense concerns a person’s character expressed through conduct.

Kanaath is a proper name, referring to a particular person or place identified by that name rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 32:42. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain further details about whom or what Kanaath identifies. Its precise significance in that passage therefore depends on reading the verse and its broader context.

Karmilia is a proper name, given in the gloss as “Karmēlia; Karmilia.” It identifies a named individual or designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 3:1. The available lexical information establishes the name’s identity and spelling, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the person’s particular role in that passage.

This adjective means “very bitter,” describing something intensely harsh or bitter rather than mildly unpleasant. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Samuel 17:8, so its normal biblical use is represented by a single occurrence. The word’s force is emphatic: it strengthens the idea of bitterness and presents it as especially severe. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context.

This noun means “boasting”—speaking proudly about oneself, one’s possessions, or achievements. It describes self-exalting speech or the attitude expressed through such speech, rather than simple recognition of something good. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 10 times, including passages in Ezekiel, Proverbs, Jeremiah, and 1 Chronicles. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding words, but its central idea remains proud self-praise or confidence expressed in speech.

This adjective describes something that fills the world or is worldwide in reach. It points to broad extent rather than a local or limited scope, expressing a presence that spreads throughout the inhabited world. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 15:31. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is something world-filling or worldwide.

This word means “dog,” referring to the familiar animal. It is a noun used throughout the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, with 35 occurrences in this LXX corpus. The word can refer simply to dogs as animals, while its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and comparison being made. It appears across historical books, poetry, prophecy, and wisdom literature, showing that its basic meaning remains recognizable across different kinds of biblical writing.

This noun refers to an “enrolment” or “census,” meaning a formal registering or counting of people. It names the act or record of listing a population, rather than describing an individual person. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 2:28. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains a population enrolment or census.

This Greek LXX verb means “oil” or “get rich.” It can describe applying oil, or becoming prosperous and well supplied. The word appears eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, so its exact sense depends on the sentence in which it occurs. Its basic idea is connected either with oil as a substance or with becoming enriched. In one recorded rendering, it is translated “oil.”

This verb means “deliver”: to bring someone out of danger, difficulty, or an unwanted condition. It describes an action performed for another person rather than a thing or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Exodus and Job, so its normal meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The precise force in either passage depends on how the sentence uses the verb. Its basic idea remains the act of delivering or bringing someone out.

Matekka is a proper name: it identifies a named person or place rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears twice, in Numbers 33:28 and 33:29. The available lexical meaning is simply “Matekka,” so no broader meaning or translation sense should be added. Its precise reference is determined by the surrounding passage, not by the name alone.

This word is a proper name referring to Menelaus, a person named in the Greek text. It is not a common term describing an action, quality, or object, but identifies an individual. The name appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Maccabees 4:39. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself establishes the person’s identification, while the passage supplies the details about him.

Merimōth, rendered Merimoth, is a proper name referring to a person. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is chiefly its identification of an individual named Merimoth. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Ezra 8:33. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain that person’s particular role in the passage; the name itself functions as a personal designation.

This noun refers to a memorial or tomb—a place connected with remembering and burying the dead. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for burial places and the sites where the dead are laid to rest. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek LXX corpus, with most occurrences in the Old Testament and several in Genesis. Its basic sense remains a physical memorial or tomb, while the surrounding passage determines the particular emphasis. “Tomb” is also an attested English rendering.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Mysarchēs” or “Misarkhis,” rather than a common term describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person in the Greek LXX material. It occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 5:24. The available wording preserves the name in two transliterated forms but does not provide an additional descriptive meaning or explain the person’s role.

Naaliēl is a proper name, referring to a specific named entity rather than expressing a general idea or action. It is also given as “Naalil,” an alternate form of the name. In the Greek LXX, it occurs twice, both times in Numbers 21:19. The name’s particular referent in that passage cannot be identified from the word alone without the surrounding verse text.

Nambra, also rendered Namvra, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named subject in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Numbers 32:3. The available information establishes the name’s wording and use as a designation, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain more specifically whom or what it identifies.

Nikanōr, also rendered Nikanor, is a personal name rather than a word describing an object, action, or quality. It identifies individual people in the Greek Old Testament tradition, functioning as a proper name. This name occurs 43 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing especially in 1 and 2 Maccabees, with one further occurrence in 4 Maccabees. Its precise reference changes from passage to passage, so the surrounding verse is needed to identify which Nikanor is meant.

This noun refers to friendly gifts or tribute—something offered as a gesture of goodwill, honor, or acknowledgment. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Ezra 1:6. The word therefore names an offering presented to another person rather than an action or quality. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense centers on gifts given in friendship or as tribute.

It means “with the entire root,” describing something done completely from its root or foundation. As an adverb, it modifies an action by showing that the action reaches the whole root rather than affecting only part of it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 3:13. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the word itself emphasizes totality and thoroughness at the deepest point.

This Greek LXX verb means “produce sour grapes.” It describes the action of bringing forth grapes with a sour quality, rather than simply naming a grape. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Isaiah 18:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains focused on the result produced: sour grapes. This rare word points to an outcome defined by the character of what the crop yields.

This noun describes a person who is twenty-five years old. It identifies a specific age rather than an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears seven times, all in the book of Numbers, where it serves as an age designation. Its meaning is precise and straightforward: the person being described has reached twenty-five years of age. The word’s exact role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains the same.

This LXX Greek verb means “head around” or “go around,” describing movement from one place or direction around another. It presents an action rather than a person or object, so its exact force depends on what is being moved and where it goes in the sentence. The verb occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, including passages in Isaiah, Ezekiel, Amos, and 2 Maccabees. Its central idea remains movement around or onward by a changed route.

This word means “surrounding territory”—the land or region around a particular place. It can function as a noun for the nearby area or as a description of something belonging to that surrounding region. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 21 times, showing a repeated focus on geographical areas around cities, lands, or other locations. Its precise force in any verse depends on which place or region it describes, but its central idea remains the territory lying around something else.

gl: place where many people assemble; place of burial;
d: place where many people assemble; place of burial;

e.t: This Greek Old Testament word refers to a place where many people are gathered, especially a place of burial. It is a noun used for a collective burial ground or a site associated with many people together. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, including passages in Jeremiah, Ezekiel, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means to worship or bow down, describing an outward act of honoring or revering someone. It can express submission through physically bowing before the one being honored. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Exodus 11:8. Its central idea remains an act of humble worship or submission, while the surrounding verse determines exactly how that action functions in context.

This verb means “lament at,” expressing sorrow directed toward a person, event, or situation. It describes an act of grieving or mourning in response to something. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 19:3. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central sense is an expression of sorrow concerning something. It is an action word, describing what someone does when responding mournfully to what has happened.

gl: one who plays the first part; chief actor
d: one who plays the first part; chief actor

e.t: This Greek LXX noun means “one who plays the first part” or “chief actor”—the leading person in an event, struggle, or public action. It identifies someone who takes the foremost role rather than a minor or supporting part. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains a person occupying the leading place.

Saaria is a proper name, referring to a person named Saaria rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 8:26. Because the surrounding passage is not included here, the name itself gives the clearest meaning: it identifies someone by name. Its precise role in that passage must be understood from the verse and its surrounding context.

Sameri is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 11:45. The available rendering preserves the name as “Sameri,” so no broader lexical meaning is indicated. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person identified there.

Sarath is a proper name, referring to a named place or person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Joshua 19:41, and is rendered “Sarath.” Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the specific referent cannot be identified more precisely from this word alone. Its role is therefore simply to preserve the name Sarath within the account recorded in Joshua.

This Greek LXX noun means “moth,” the small insect associated with damaging or consuming clothing and other materials. It is used as an ordinary name for the creature, rather than as a description of a person or action. The word occurs 18 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, including passages in Job, Proverbs, Isaiah, Wisdom, and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse comes from the surrounding sentence and the object connected with the moth.

This Greek LXX noun means “sheltered,” describing someone or something kept under protection or cover. It expresses the condition of being shielded rather than exposed. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, in Nehemiah 4:7. Because the surrounding verse text is not included, its exact reference in that passage cannot be explained further; its basic lexical sense remains a protected or sheltered condition.

This noun refers to preparing or dressing—the act of getting something ready or arranging it appropriately. Its basic sense is practical and descriptive, naming preparation rather than a person, object, or abstract belief. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at Ecclesiastes 10:1. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise role in that verse cannot be described further; its lexical meaning remains “preparing; dressing.”

This noun means “insemination,” referring to the placing or depositing of seed for reproduction. It names a reproductive act rather than a person, object, or quality.
